title: Three turnings
hookLine: a Mahayana map of three turnings of the wheel; other schools map it differently

cards: In a deer park near Benares, the Buddha gives his first teaching to a few old companions who had once walked away from him: the four truths, the middle way. You met that morning back in year one.
The Pali text says that when he finished, the cry went up from the earth to the heavens: the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling. The schools took that picture in different directions.
Some say the wheel turned once, at the deer park, and has been rolling ever since. Others say it turned again, and then a third time.

teach.h: THE WHEEL SET ROLLING AT THE DEER PARK.

teach.b: In the Pali canon this talk is the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, setting the wheel of dhamma in motion; Rhys Davids gave it a grand English title, The Foundation of the Kingdom of Righteousness.
Every map today starts here. Second, the Mahayana map.
A Mahayana scripture, the Samdhinirmocana Sutra, describes the teaching turning in three stages. First, the four truths, taught at the deer park.
Second, the teaching of emptiness, found in the Perfection of Wisdom sutras. Third, a turning that clarifies the second, carefully distinguishing what is meant literally from what needs interpreting.
That map became important in Tibet. Third, maps inside the map.

Tibetan schools don't agree on which turning is final. Some hold that the second, on emptiness, is the definitive word; others give that place to the third, and each sets out its reasons in long, careful debate.
In China, Tiantai teachers drew a different map again, arranging the sutras into periods of the Buddha's teaching life. Fourth, the Theravada view.
The Theravada keeps the Pali canon as the Buddha's word and doesn't accept the later sutras into it.
For a Theravada teacher, the wheel set rolling at the deer park is the wheel, still turning, with no second or third.
Each map orders a huge body of teaching, and they can lie side by side without one being torn up.

how: Tibetan monastic colleges study the three turnings in depth and debate which is definitive, while Theravada teachers keep the Pali canon and its first discourse at the deer park as the turning of the wheel.

o: a Tibetan prayer wheel spun three times for luck
three sermons the Buddha gave at the deer park
a Mahayana map of the teaching in three stages

p: the four truths, at the deer park

s: every Buddhist school uses the three-turnings map
it's a Mahayana map. Theravada keeps one wheel; Tiantai in China drew yet another map.
Tibetan schools agree on which turning is final
some give that place to the second turning, others to the third, each with its reasons.
Rhys Davids called the first talk The Foundation of the Kingdom of Righteousness
his English title for the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta.

games.q: a Tibetan teacher shows you the three turnings. that afternoon a Theravada monk tells you the wheel turned once. what do you do?
o: work out which of them is right before going further.
lay both maps side by side: each orders the teaching its own way.
games.why: the schools themselves do this: each explains its own map, and even the Tibetan schools weigh the turnings differently.

practice: Picture the deer park as a small circle. From it, draw one long line, the Theravada wheel rolling on, and beside it three rings, the Mahayana turnings, side by side like two maps of the same coastline.
Rest with your breath and look at both, and if an urge to pick a winner comes, let it rest too.

wordCard.voice: Three turnings. A Mahayana map of the teaching in three stages: the four truths, emptiness, and a clarifying turning. Other schools draw the map differently. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit dharmacakra (Pali dhammacakka): the wheel of the teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: maps differ. A map shows how its maker walks the land. Rest well.
